overview: This file consists of a seven-page American consular report on commercial aviation in the Japanese-controlled Kwantung Leased Territory during 1930. Prepared by Consul Cabot Coville at Dairen, it describes restrictions on flying near fortified areas, the territory’s airport and weather conditions, and the subsidized Japan Air Transport Company service linking Dairen with Tokyo through Korea and western Japan. It provides unusually detailed schedules, distances, fares, baggage and freight charges, passenger and air-mail statistics, aircraft specifications, and observations on the market for American airplanes, while noting that information about military aviation was unavailable.

subfiles.title: Aviation in 1930: Kwantung Leased Territory
subfiles.from: Cabot Coville, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: U.S. Department of State, with copies to American offices at Tokyo, Shanghai, and Mukden
subfiles.about: A consular survey of commercial aviation facilities, regulation, traffic, routes, equipment, and market conditions in the Kwantung Leased Territory during 1930.
subfiles.summary: Coville reports that commercial aviation in the territory consisted of a single subsidized Japan Air Transport Company route connecting Dairen with Tokyo through Pyongyang, Seoul, Ulsan, Fukuoka, and Osaka. He describes stringent Japanese restrictions on flight near fortified areas, the Dairen airfield, local meteorological and topographical conditions, schedules, fares, baggage and freight rates, and air-mail service. Statistics for 1930 show low passenger loads but substantial mail traffic, with no local accidents. The report also records the use of American-made Fokker Super-Universal aircraft with Bristol Jupiter engines, some manufactured in Japan by Nakajima, and concludes that the American aircraft market was secure but unlikely to expand locally.

interest: The report offers a data-rich snapshot of civil aviation within Japan’s colonial transportation system shortly before the occupation of Manchuria transformed the region. Its route schedules, fares, traffic totals, and aircraft details permit close comparison of air travel with contemporary railway and steamship services. It is also valuable for showing how nominally commercial aviation combined government subsidy, semi-governmental control, military secrecy, and restrictions on foreign access, while relying on American aircraft and a mixture of British- and Japanese-produced engines.
